The scope of work is to remove and replace the existing walk-in cooler and freezer at both schools; the units are original to each building and are becoming unreliable due to their condition and the limited availability of replacement parts.

Carson recommends Stafford-Smith, Inc. as the low qualified bidder in the amount of $227,606.32. The project has been approved by the State of Michigan (Michigan Department of Education) for use with Food Service Funds. Upon board approval, a purchase order will be issued to Stafford-Smith; project commencement will be determined by equipment delivery timelines and the availability of TSD Food Service Operations to accommodate the work. Trustees rate both the board as a whole and themselves on a 4-to-1 scale across six domains of effective governance - Coherence, Governance Mindset, Systems Thinking, Strategic Focus, Deep Learning, and Managing Manner - and brainstorm one or two concrete improvements per area to guide a workshop discussion.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A blank board self-evaluation template for the Troy School District Board of Education, covering the 2022-2023 school year. The form's concepts and language are drawn from Davis Campbell and Michael Fullan's text, 'The Governance Core: School Boards, Superintendents, and Schools Working Together.'

Purpose
To have trustees reflect on the board's and their own performance over the prior 12 months and translate that reflection into concrete actions for improvement over the next 12 months. Completed forms also seed a constructive discussion at a board workshop.

Six governance domains assessed
1. Coherence - shared depth of understanding about the nature of the work
2. Governance Mindset - core understanding of basic governance principles
3. Strategic Focus
4. Systems Thinking
5. Deep Learning
6. Managing Manner

Rating scale
Each attribute is rated for both 'The Board' and 'Me':
- 4 = a foundational strength of this board
- 3 = generally good
- 2 = needs improvement
- 1 = a critical weakness of this board
Each section also gets a summary 'gestalt' rating (not a strict average) plus one or two improvement ideas expressed as positive, concrete actions.

Sample attributes
The Coherence section lists 15 attributes, including trustees' emotional commitment and 'ownership' of the strategic vision, reinforcing a culture of trust through reliability and competence, maintaining confidentiality on personnel and closed-session content, avoiding single-issue agendas or representing specific constituencies, abiding by policy even when voting against a resolution, and not intervening at the administrative level to solve constituents' problems.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A governance self-assessment tool used by the Troy School District Board of Education for the 2022-2023 school year, provided in the December 5, 2023 Workshop materials. The form was developed from the concepts and language established by Davis Campbell and Michael Fullan in their text 'The Governance Core: School Boards, Superintendents, and Schools Working Together,' and in many cases the attribute wording is pulled directly from that book.

The stated purpose is for the board to reflect on its performance as a collective body and for each trustee to reflect on their own performance over the past 12 months, then use that introspection to develop concrete actions for improving the team's performance over the next 12 months. Trustees are instructed to complete the form in advance and bring it to a workshop, where the board ratings guide a constructive discussion.

The assessment is organized around six areas Campbell and Fullan identify as central to high-functioning school boards: (1) Coherence - individuals' shared depth of understanding about the nature of the work; (2) Governance Mindset - core understanding of the basic principles of governance; (3) Strategic Focus; (4) Systems Thinking; (5) Deep Learning; and (6) Managing Manner. For each area, trustees rate specific attributes on a four-point scale for both 'The Board' and 'Me': 4 = a foundational strength of this board; 3 = generally good; 2 = needs improvement; 1 = a critical weakness of this board. At the end of each section, trustees provide a holistic summary 'gestalt' rating (explicitly not required to be a mathematical average) and brainstorm one or two concrete, positively framed improvement ideas.

The Coherence section enumerates 15 attributes, among them: whether individual trustees have a depth of understanding of the work; whether they demonstrate an emotional commitment such that the board 'owns' rather than 'observes' the strategic vision; whether they reinforce a culture of trust through reliability ('I keep my word') and competence ('I am skilled at follow-through'); whether they believe fellow trustees' motivations are honorable, ethical, and honest; whether they maintain confidentiality rules on personnel and closed-session content; whether they avoid representing specific constituencies or pursuing single-issue agendas; whether they abide by board policy even after voting against a resolution; and whether they avoid intervening at the administrative level to solve problems for constituents. A subsequent Governance Mindset section begins with attributes on the board's unity of purpose and shared moral imperative - a relentless commitment to the learning of all students. The extracted copy is the blank template, without completed ratings.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A recognition script prepared for the second "TSD Mission Moment" at the Troy Board of Education's Regular Meeting on December 12, 2023, honoring the district's WEB teacher leaders. WEB stands for "Where Everybody Belongs," a middle school orientation and transition program designed to welcome sixth graders and make them feel comfortable throughout the first year of their middle school experience. The program is built on the belief that students can help other students succeed; it trains mentors drawn from the eighth grade to serve as WEB Leaders. As positive role models, these WEB Leaders mentor and guide sixth graders, helping them discover what it takes to be successful during the transition to middle school and facilitating sixth-grade success.

The script emphasizes that WEB also functions as an anti-bullying program: it provides a cadre of student leaders who look for bullying behavior and help stop it, giving older students permission to be aware of and report any negative behavior they observe, thereby creating a safer school environment for everyone. Through the program, students learn that people at school care about them and their success.

The eight teacher leaders recognized are Philip Lewan, Allyson Pagnani, Emily Stetson, Judy Morgan, Maria Mendola, Jaclynn Parker, Cortney Walls, and Raymond Torres. It frames the district's data sources - the SAT Suite (SAT 11, PSAT 8) and M-STEP 3-7 for standardized data; Fountas & Pinnell, CommonLit, and NWEA for benchmarking; and AP results and graduation rate as exit data - and details SAT/PSAT math and reading-writing subcategories. What it is
A slide presentation, "Student Assessment Data," given to the Troy School District Board of Education in December 2023 on student achievement measures over time.

Data framework
- Standardized: SAT Suite of Assessments - SAT 11 (Scholastic Aptitude Test), PSAT 8; M-STEP grades 3-7
- Instructional/benchmarking: Fountas & Pinnell (ELA K-5), CommonLit (ELA 6-12), NWEA - Math (grade 6-Algebra 1)
- Exit: Advanced Placement assessments; graduation rate

Why SAT 11
A national norm-referenced assessment with consistent content and structure over time (unlike M-STEP/MEAP variance), a leading college-admissions test, and a linked suite spanning grades 8-11. It shows programmatic impact over time and allows state/county/school/student-group comparison, including Oakland County performance for EBRW and Math with economically disadvantaged (ED) students.

Subcategories analyzed
- Math: Heart of Algebra; Passport to Advanced Math; Problem Solving and Data Analysis
- Reading/Writing (EBRW): Command of Evidence; Expression of Ideas; Standard English Conventions; Words in Context
Results are color-coded green (proficient/advanced), yellow (partially proficient), red (not proficient).

Math benchmarking changes
With the new K-8 math curriculum, the district will use PSAT 8 Math as one data set and introduce NWEA that winter as a second, norm-referenced computer-adaptive assessment given during math class, replacing district-created benchmarks. Program evaluation is in partnership with Illustrative Math.

A PowerPoint presentation titled "Student Assessment Data" delivered at the Troy School District Board of Education meeting in December 2023 (the file is a version 2, roughly 16 slides). Its theme is "Reviewing Consistent Measures Over Time," presenting the district's framework of achievement and benchmarking data to the board.

Data sources framework: The presentation organizes measures into three groups. Standardized assessment data comprises the SAT Suite of Assessments - the SAT 11 (Scholastic Aptitude Test, grade 11), the PSAT 8 - and M-STEP for grades 3-7. Instructional/benchmarking data comprises Fountas & Pinnell (ELA, grades K-5), CommonLit (ELA, grades 6-12), and NWEA - Math (grade 6 through Algebra 1). Exit data comprises Advanced Placement assessments and the graduation rate.

Rationale for SAT 11: The deck argues the SAT 11 is valuable because it is a national norm-referenced assessment with consistent content and structure over time (contrasted with M-STEP/MEAP variance), is among the leading collegiate admissions assessments, and is part of a suite with linkages from grade 8 to grade 11. It states the assessment shows programmatic impact over time, provides comparison data across state/county/school/student group, and offers transparency. Specific comparison slides address Oakland County Performance on SAT 11 EBRW (Evidence-Based Reading and Writing) with ED (economically disadvantaged) students and Oakland County Performance on SAT 11 Math with ED.

Subcategory analysis: The presentation explains that each assessment has subcategories used to examine trends in narrower instructional areas, while noting that at the system level this data is not useful for addressing specific individual student learning needs. Defined SAT Math subcategories are Heart of Algebra (linear equations, systems, and functions), Passport to Advanced Math (structure of expressions, complex equations, building functions), and Problem Solving and Data Analysis (ratios, percentages, proportional reasoning, and interpreting graphical/statistical data). Defined SAT Evidence-Based Reading and Writing subcategories are Command of Evidence, Expression of Ideas, Standard English Conventions, and Words in Context. Subcategory comparison slides for both Math and EBRW use a color key: green = proficient or advanced, yellow = partially proficient, red = not proficient.

Math benchmarking and curriculum change: A section titled "Math Benchmarking - PSAT 8 & Future NWEA" describes how, as the district moves forward with its new K-8 math curriculum, it will use PSAT 8 Math performance as one data set to understand student growth over time. That winter the district planned to introduce NWEA as a second data set for math performance, replacing district-created benchmark assessments. Detailed judge feedback for Troy School District's entry in the 2023 Gold Medallion Awards, a Michigan school public-relations recognition program, evaluating the district's communications campaign tied to its bond effort. The entry is scored across three rubric sections, each with a numeric average and multiple judges' comments.

Research (4.83/5.00): Judges called the section very thorough, covering a variety of aspects of the program and types of research, with survey feedback on building needs providing necessary primary research and objectives that are SMART and aligned to the research. They praised the impressive mix of primary and secondary data and "fantastic research reaching all stakeholders and outside assessments." Suggestions included adding charts/graphs from the community survey for visual variety, referencing the community's voting demographics and whether survey results aligned with them, explicitly stating and labeling the project goal, distinguishing which items were primary/secondary and formal/informal along with specific methodologies, and tightening the wordier third objective (which one judge said should end at "...motivate their families/staff to vote").

Planning (4.67/5.00): Judges described a very detailed plan with set roles, objectives, strategies, and tactics, and commended tying the campaign into the district's strategic plan and completing an environmental scan. They appreciated the identification of target audiences and the stated recognition that "it was crucial to be flexible and be able to adapt to changing conditions as they developed," calling that a hallmark of a public relations professional. Recommendations urged tying each strategy to an objective and fully detailing strategies (how objectives are carried out) and tactics (the specific tools, such as yard signs or billboards), and outlining the five planning elements that frame communication plans: goals; public identification; objectives; strategies; and tactics. Judges also noted the budget and team roles/responsibilities were well included.

Implementation (4.67/5.00): Judges observed that initial survey feedback and the community survey surfaced phrases and needs that resonated with stakeholders and were turned into clear key messages targeted to appropriate audiences through research-proven outlets. They highlighted the idea of having a real estate agent create a video to promote the value of the district, and praised the visually appealing, attention-grabbing graphics and well-executed branding.

Foresite Design was solely responsible for the synthetic-turf system portion of the project and had recently performed similar work for the district's stadium synthetic-turf replacement. The specification and design for the synthetic-turf systems — covering both the auxiliary turf and the baseball/softball fields — were written to be inclusive of all major manufacturers, by design, to ensure a competitive bid process.

AstroTurf-Great Lakes submitted three: VA#1, a '3D3' enhanced synthetic-turf system with a proprietary 'RootZone' feature, for the auxiliary turf fields only; VA#2, a Brock SP14 shock pad in lieu of the Schmitz Pro Play 20; and VA#3, SMG TCA 1400 grooming equipment for maintenance. Shaw Sports Turf submitted VA#1, its 'Game On' system for all fields, which allows colors to be tufted in at the factory, eliminating roughly 90% of cut/sewn inlays (lines, numbers, logos) and the additional cost for logos (Alternate #1 on the bid price form). The Shaw VA applies to both the auxiliary turf fields and the baseball and softball fields, includes the cost for a Shaw NXT Pad in lieu of the Schmitz Pro Play 20 shock pad, and represents a cost reduction for the baseball and softball fields due to installation efficiencies (factory-tufted lines and logos versus additional materials and on-site labor to cut and glue).

Post-bid interviews were conducted by Barton Malow and Foresite Design to verify bid thoroughness. A post-bid discussion was held with TSD Athletics (Tim Fulcher, Todd Heugh, and Shane Hynes), TSD Operations (Larry Franckowiak and Rob Carson), and Foresite Design (Mike Sims). Mike Sims led an unbiased discussion and provided professional insight based on his knowledge and experience of all the systems.

The discussion summary records that, starting with the auxiliary turf fields, a unanimous consensus identified Shaw's VA#1 'Game On' as the preferred selection due to the reduction in seams/inlays and because it would put the same synthetic-turf system on the auxiliary fields as in the district's stadiums. The ball-fields discussion likewise resulted in a unanimous decision for Shaw's VA#1 'Game On,' citing the reduction in seams/inlays and the lowest bid price. A memorandum on Troy School District Technology Services letterhead (4420 Livernois; phone 248.823.5060) from Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, dated December 20, 2023, transmitting the recommendation and cost breakdown for the district's five-year Fiber Maintenance Agreement covering 2024-2029.

The memo frames fiber maintenance as an E-rate-eligible project for which all work except new builds qualifies for 40% reimbursement. It explains that E-rate rules require the district to competitively bid maintenance of its district-owned fiber, and that bidders must submit an annual maximum estimate; any amount spent above the awarded vendor's estimated maximum is not eligible for reimbursement. Soggs stresses that the vendor whose estimate appears extremely high actually has the lowest cost, because its maximum estimate exceeds the district's current annual expenditures and therefore ensures that every dollar spent on maintenance remains reimbursable.

She emphasizes that the dollar amount is only a maximum and that the district pays only for actual hours and materials used, noting that some years require little maintenance while others bring ice storms, road work, new construction, car accidents, DTE pole audits, and squirrel chews. After thoroughly evaluating the proposals received, the memo concludes that FiberLink has the overall lowest rates.

The recommendation for FiberLink rests on four points: its lowest cost-per-hour labor rates; its geographic proximity to Troy, which yields quicker response times and fewer hours charged for travel; a maximum estimate that ensures every dollar is eligible for reimbursement; and a long-standing relationship with the district, including familiarity with the district's fiber routes (often without needing to consult maps) and a record of excellent past service and response times. The memo closes by noting that this is an annually budgeted general fund expenditure. It accompanies a separate detailed cost comparison and an outside recommendation letter supporting the same conclusion.

The memo carries a printed date of January 3, 2023, but recaps work performed from March through November 2023.

OCBA Landscape Architects joined the Phase 1 design team, alongside TMP Architects and Troy School District staff, in March 2023. The effort built on a playground review audit completed in 2020 by Landscape Architects & Planners, Inc. and J.C. Walker & Sons Corp., which identified and documented non-compliance with federal standards and other deficiencies in existing equipment and playground surfacing at all of the district's elementary schools and recommended replacing many existing play pieces.

The memo details the process: on March 15 the design team met with the TSD Playground Committee to review scope, budget, and guidelines; on April 14 and April 27 OCBA staff visited all six Phase 1 elementary schools, meeting Troy Schools staff including principals and special education teachers. At Troy Union Elementary, Barnard Elementary, and Martell Elementary, OCBA staff additionally met with students to review their conceptual playground design projects. In spring 2023 TSD issued a playground survey to district parents, whose responses were shared with the design team. The team then typically met bi-weekly to develop equipment palettes and conceptual plans, with principals given multiple chances to give feedback; final plans were established in November and coordinated with site-work plans to be bid during the winter by Barton Malow.

On vendors, the memo notes the existing playgrounds used equipment from GameTime, Playworld, and Landscape Structures, all IPEMA-certified firms with which OCBA had prior successful projects. To reduce future maintenance coordination for TSD Facilities staff, OCBA recommended working with a maximum of two playground companies. TSD Facilities staff requested Midstates Recreation (Playworld) based on prior successful installations; OCBA also spoke with Sinclair Recreation (GameTime) and Penchura (Landscape Structures), and Sinclair Recreation had the design and installation capacity for the proposed Phase 1 and Phase 2 work. Sinclair Recreation (GameTime) and Midstates Recreation (Playworld) were selected. Both belong to national purchasing cooperatives, Omnia Partners and Sourcewell respectively, which solicit and vet competitive bid pricing, allowing TSD to obtain certified equipment at cooperative pricing while avoiding a separate bidding process and reducing design time, expense, and management effort. The remaining step described is selecting color schemes for each playground area, which each school was coordinating internally for inclusion in the final order.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Background and process memorandum from Rachel Hughes-Nilsson, Associate at OCBA Landscape Architects (OCBA), addressed to Rick West, Deputy Superintendent of the Troy School District. The subject is the Troy School District Phase 1 Elementary Playground Improvements in Troy, Michigan. The memo is dated 3 January 2023, although it describes activities extending through the following November, and it accompanies agenda item 11.B at the January 16, 2024 board meeting.

OCBA joined the Phase 1 Elementary Playground Improvements design team, alongside TMP Architects and Troy School District staff, in March 2023. Before OCBA's involvement, a playground review audit had been completed in 2020 by Landscape Architects & Planners, Inc. and J.C. Walker & Sons Corp. That assessment identified and documented non-compliance with federal standards and other deficiencies in existing equipment and playground surfacing at all of the district's elementary schools, and recommended replacing many existing play pieces.

The memo details an extensive planning and community-input process. On March 15 the design team met the TSD Playground Committee to review overall scope, budget and guidelines. On April 14 and April 27, OCBA staff visited all six Phase 1 elementary schools to review existing sites and equipment, meeting with district staff including principals and special-education teachers. At Troy Union, Barnard and Martell Elementary Schools, OCBA additionally met with students to review their conceptual playground design projects and discuss equipment ideas. In spring 2023, TSD issued a playground survey to district parents, and the responses were recorded and shared with the design team, which met roughly bi-weekly.

On vendor selection, OCBA recommended working with a maximum of two playground companies to reduce future maintenance coordination for TSD Facilities staff. The existing playgrounds contained equipment from GameTime, Playworld and Landscape Structures, all IPEMA-certified manufacturers. TSD Facilities requested that Midstates Recreation (Playworld) be one vendor, based on prior successful repairs and installations. OCBA also spoke with Sinclair Recreation (GameTime) and Penchura (Landscape Structures); Sinclair had the design and installation capacity for the proposed Phase 1 and Phase 2 work. Sinclair Recreation (GameTime) belongs to the Omnia Partners purchasing cooperative, while Midstates Recreation (Playworld) belongs to Sourcewell.

The memo explains the rationale for cooperative purchasing: cooperatives solicit and organize competitive pricing across many vendors and products, vet vendors' ability to supply on schedule, and allow an additional discount because the vendor has already completed the bid process with the cooperative rather than each owner. For TSD, this approach ensures receipt of exactly the certified playground equipment required, avoids the risk of a lower-quality or uncertified product, reduces overall design time and expense, and cuts Facilities' management effort by limiting the number of companies handling repairs.

Once GameTime and Playworld were identified as the selected vendors, the design team created multiple equipment palettes and conceptual plans meeting the established guidelines; principals and staff reviewed and gave feedback, revisions were made, and final plans were established in November. Those plans were coordinated with the site-work plans to be bid over the winter by Barton Malow. The final step, once pricing is approved, is each school selecting its playground color schemes, which will be included in the final order.

It documents the design collaboration and the professional evaluation that led to selecting Shaw Sports Turf's voluntary alternate.

The RFP covered athletic-field renovation work at Athens and Troy High Schools. The plans, scope of work and blueprints were a collaboration between TMP Architecture, Foresite Design and PBA Engineering. Foresite Design was solely responsible for the synthetic-turf system portion of the project and had recently performed similar work for the district's stadium synthetic-turf replacement.

The specification and design for the synthetic-turf systems, covering both the auxiliary turf fields and the baseball/softball fields, was written to be inclusive of all major manufacturers. This was intentional, to ensure a competitive bid process. Two of the three manufacturers that bid submitted voluntary alternatives unique to each: Astroturf-Great Lakes and Shaw Sports Turf.

Astroturf-Great Lakes submitted three voluntary alternatives: VA#1, a "3D3" enhanced synthetic-turf system with a proprietary "RootZone" feature, for the auxiliary turf fields only; VA#2, a Brock SP14 shock pad in lieu of the Schmitz Pro Play 20 (both are shock pads installed under the turf on the auxiliary fields); and VA#3, SMG TCA 1400 grooming equipment for maintenance.

Shaw Sports Turf submitted VA#1, its "Game On" system for all fields. This system allows colors to be tufted in at the factory, eliminating roughly 90% of cut-and-sewn inlays (lines, numbers and logos) and the additional cost for logos (Alternate #1 on the bid price form). It applies to both the auxiliary turf fields and the baseball and softball fields, and includes the cost for a Shaw NXT Pad in lieu of the Schmitz Pro Play 20 shock pad. On the baseball and softball fields the "Game On" system is a net cost reduction, because tufting lines and logos at the factory avoids the additional materials and on-site labor to cut and glue inlays.

Post-bid interviews were conducted by Barton Malow and Foresite Design to verify bid thoroughness. A post-bid discussion followed with TSD Athletics staff (Tim Fulcher, Todd Heugh and Shane Hynes), TSD Operations staff (Larry Franckowiak and Rob Carson) and Foresite Design (Mike Sims). Mike Sims led what the document describes as an unbiased discussion, providing professional insight based on knowledge and experience of all the systems.

The discussion began with the auxiliary turf fields, where a unanimous consensus identified Shaw's VA#1 "Game On" as the preferred selection, owing to the reduction in seams and inlays and the fact that it would give the district the same synthetic-turf system on its auxiliary fields as in its stadiums. The ball-fields discussion likewise resulted in a unanimous decision for Shaw's VA#1 "Game On," based on the reduction in seams and inlays and the lowest bid price. The preface thus supports awarding the synthetic-turf category to Shaw Integrated & Turf Solutions with Voluntary Alternate #1 included.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A bid-evaluation spreadsheet prepared to support agenda item 11.D at the Troy School District Board of Education's January 16, 2024 organizational and regular meeting, comparing three vendors competing to maintain the district-owned fiber cabling: FiberLink, AmComm, and Turn Key (Turnkey Network Solutions).

The worksheet lists each bidder's rates across six categories plus an optional annual "ride out." Maximum E-rate allowances (the annual base figures) are $115,000.00 for FiberLink, $75,000.00 for AmComm, and $58,337.29 for Turn Key. MissDig office-locate charges per ticket are $9.75 (FiberLink), $28.00 (AmComm), and $15.00 (Turn Key); MissDig field-locate charges per ticket are $82, $125, and $85 respectively. Emergency-call pricing is $78-$90 per hour for FiberLink, $2,200 per call plus $75-$150 per hour for AmComm, and $182-$192 for Turn Key. Standard hourly rates are $78 (FiberLink), $75-$150 (AmComm), and $110-$125 (Turn Key). Truck fees are $150 per truck (FiberLink), $250 per hour (AmComm), and included in the labor rate (Turn Key). A note records that Turn Key also requires a monthly retainer for fiber-outage response equating to $3,600.00 annually, and that quoted hourly rates vary by labor type (laborer, lineman, supervisor) and exclude overtime or holiday premiums.

For historical context, the document states the district had 911 MissDig tickets in the prior year, with a maintenance person on-site for a total of 106 hours, plus two emergency repairs requiring 234 man-hours; the annual expense for 2022-23 was $51,074.02.

A "Major Repairs Cost Comparison" models four actual district scenarios -- Hill Repair, Costello Repair, I-75 & Rochester Lash, and a Splice Case -- across straight-time hours, overtime hours, and truck hours/days. FiberLink's per-project totals are $2,640.00, $1,944.00, $7,840.50, and $735.00, summing to $13,159.50. AmComm's totals are $11,770.00, $7,805.00, $18,041.25, and $5,050.00, summing to $42,666.25. Turn Key's totals are $5,460.00, $4,186.00, $17,244.50, and $1,365.00, summing to $28,255.50.

A separate "2022-23 MissDig Cost Comparison" models the 911 office locates and 234 hours of field locates. FiberLink: $8,882.25 office plus $18,252.00 field, no after-hours premium, total $27,134.25. AmComm: $25,508.00 office plus $29,250.00 field, total $54,758.00. Turn Key: $13,665.00 office plus $25,740.00 field, total $39,405.00.

Across both modeled comparisons FiberLink produces the lowest actual cost even though it carries the highest maximum E-rate allowance, illustrating the evaluation's central point that a higher maximum estimate paired with lower unit rates best protects the district's E-rate reimbursement eligibility. The worksheet accompanies the recommendation letter and resolution awarding Bid #2324-05 to Fiber Link, Inc.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum dated December 20, 2023 from Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, transmitting the recommendation letter and cost breakdown for a five-year Fiber Maintenance Agreement spanning 2024-2029. The memo originates from Technology Services at 4420 Livernois (phone 248.823.5060) and accompanies agenda item 11.D at the Board's January 16, 2024 meeting.

Soggs explains that fiber maintenance is an E-rate-eligible project, and that all work except new builds is eligible for 40% reimbursement. E-rate rules require the district to competitively bid out maintenance for its district-owned fiber; this process is what preserves the district's eligibility to receive 40% reimbursement on maintenance and repair expenses. Under E-rate, the district must obtain an annual MAXIMUM estimate from bidders, and any amount spent above the awarded vendor's estimated maximum is not eligible for reimbursement.

The memo stresses a counterintuitive point: the numbers estimated by responding vendors vary greatly, and the vendor that appears extremely high actually has the lowest cost. That vendor's maximum estimate exceeds the district's current annual expenditures, which ensures that every dollar the district spends on maintenance remains eligible for reimbursement. Soggs notes that the dollar amount is only a maximum estimate and that the district pays only for the actual hours and materials used. Some years bring very little maintenance or emergency work, while others bring ice storms, road work, new construction, car accidents, DTE pole audits, and squirrel chews.

Having thoroughly evaluated the proposals received, Soggs reports that FiberLink has the overall lowest rates. Beyond having the lowest labor rates, FiberLink is closest geographically to Troy, which provides quicker response times and fewer hours charged for travel. FiberLink has a long-standing relationship with the district, has provided excellent service and response times in the past, and knows the district's fiber routes, often without even consulting the maps.

The memo recommends FiberLink for the agreement based on its lowest cost-per-hour rates, proximity to the district, a maximum estimate that ensures every dollar is eligible for reimbursement, and the long-standing relationship with the district. It closes by noting the work is an annually budgeted general fund expenditure.

A recommendation letter dated December 14, 2023 from Convergent Technology Partners (6197 Miller Road, Suite 4, Swartz Creek, MI 48473; phone 810.720.3820) to Beth Soggs, Technology Director of the Troy School District at 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, addressing Bid #2324-05 for maintenance of the District's fiber cabling. It accompanies agenda item 11.D at the January 16, 2024 board meeting.

The consultant reports that bids and proposals were received, opened, and read at 2:30 P.M. on November 30, 2023. Three proposals were submitted, with several voluntary alternates provided by Fiber Link. The tabulated base bids were: Fiber Link, Inc. at $115,000.00 annually; Amcomm at $75,000.00 annually; and Turnkey Network Solutions at $58,337.29 annually. All proposals were evaluated for compliance with the RFP requirements, pricing, technical solution, and acceptance of the RFP's terms and conditions; all bidders provided compliant proposals, and any exceptions or clarifications were deemed acceptable.

The letter emphasizes that the base bid is not a fixed fee for completing the year's tasks but rather an estimate the District will use to file under the E-rate program -- the dollar figure becomes the maximum amount that can be invoiced against and applied for E-rate reimbursement. Because invoices reflect actual work completed, the evaluation centered on each bidder's unit and hourly rates, with an attached comparison and a spreadsheet showing cost comparisons based on actual scenarios that have occurred in the District.

Although Turnkey appears at first glance to be the lowest bid, the letter finds that Amcomm's and Turnkey's hourly and unit rates are higher for most if not all services; that under a time-and-materials contract those higher rates would cost the District more over the life of the contract; that Fiber Link's lower hourly rates will allow the District to accomplish more and maximize the funds available under E-rate; and that Fiber Link's higher base bid will ensure all work is eligible for E-rate reimbursement and will not exhaust E-rate funds if a major incident occurs.

Based on this evaluation, Convergent Technology Partners recommends awarding the Fiber Maintenance Contract Bid #2324-05 to Fiber Link, Inc. based on its base bid of $115,000.00. Fiber Link is the contractor currently providing fiber maintenance for the District and has amassed significant knowledge of the District's network; it has proven responsive, its work is of high quality, and it is the closest bidder to the District, whereas Amcomm is headquartered in Brighton and Turnkey is located in Caledonia, nearly a two-hour drive from Troy.
